name: tgif
why: An old Xlib interactive 2D drawing tool with a long history, a close call for an old-school environment.

brief.what_it_is: Tgif (pronounced t-g-i-f) is an Xlib-based interactive 2-D drawing tool that produces vector graphics, running under X11 on Linux and most UNIX platforms (the author's page also mentions Mac OS X and Cygwin on Windows). The user draws and edits vector objects interactively in a window. The SourceForge listing describes it as a vector-based 2D drawing tool that is also a hyper-structured-graphics browser on the web. A reviewer says drawings can be exported to roughly ten graphical formats, and layers control what is shown and exported.
brief.why_it_exists: The author's framing is a drawing tool that keeps the user in control, without the many options of larger software. One reviewer describes it as easy to learn, useful for quick electrical schematics or PCB layouts, and not limited to what the designer chose. The author's page also presents it as an early hyper-structured-graphics editor and browser on the web, which became a feature in version 2.16 (Dec 3, 1994).
brief.how_it_works: The README gave no implementation detail beyond being Xlib-based with vector graphics. The author's page says that running 'tgif http://bourbon.usc.edu/tgif/index.obj' opens a hyper-graphics page, and that web browsers and servers can be configured to use tgif in hyper-graphics mode.

commands_seen.context: From the author's page: opens the tgif hyper-graphics home page in tgif's web-browser mode.

brief.install_notes: Nothing beyond the Homebrew formula was visible. The SourceForge listing shows Linux as the platform and BSD and Linux as operating systems; the author's page mentions X11 on Linux, most UNIX platforms, Mac OS X, and Cygwin. No accounts or runtimes were described. Configuring web browsers and servers for hyper-graphics mode is optional.
brief.standout: It is an old X11 vector editor that also had a hyper-graphics mode for browsing structured graphics on the web, which the author added in 2.16 in 1994. The SourceForge page lists it as first registered in 2000, with a long-running user base.
brief.status: Quiet. The SourceForge page shows Last Update 2013-04-11, and the project has been listed since 2000-04-26. The author's page is still up. No newer release date was visible in the pages I fetched, so I could not confirm the current version.
brief.caveats: Licensed under the Qt Public License (QPL). Platform support is X11-based (Linux, most UNIX, Mac OS X and Cygwin per the author's page); reviewers say it is not available on Windows natively. A SourceForge reviewer notes 'some limitations and quirks due to its history.' The listing's average is 4.5/5 from 2 reviews. The SourceForge page did not show a build or install guide.
quotes: Tgif is a vector-based 2D drawing tool. It's also a hyper-structured-graphics browser on the web.

entry.title: tgif
entry.tldr: An old X11 vector drawing editor that doubles as a browser for hyper-structured graphics, a web idea from 1994 that never caught on.
entry.deeper_look:
Tgif (pronounced t-g-i-f) is an Xlib-based interactive 2D drawing tool. You draw and edit vector objects in an X11 window, organise them with layers, and export to roughly ten graphical formats, according to one reviewer. It has no toolkit dressing, just Xlib and a lot of years behind it.

The author's framing is a drawing tool that keeps the user in control, without the many options of larger software. One long-time user calls it easy to learn and handy for quick electrical schematics or PCB layouts, and says it is not limited to what the designer chose. The same reviewer admits it has "some limitations and quirks due to its history, but it does its job well."

The odd part is the second half of the description: "It's also a hyper-structured-graphics browser on the web." Version 2.16, dated Dec 3, 1994, added this. Instead of pages of text with links, tgif can open drawings that are themselves the hypertext, with objects that link onward. Browsers and servers can be configured to hand such files to tgif. It is a small window onto a road the web did not take.

It is a piece of early-Unix-era software culture you can still run. The SourceForge page lists it as registered in 2000, and the author's page is still up.
entry.install:
brew install tgif
Needs an X11 server running (on macOS, something like XQuartz) since it draws through Xlib.

try_this.what_happens: Opens the author's hyper-graphics home page inside tgif's own browser mode, if the server is still reachable.

entry.whats_unique: A vector editor from the early X11 era that was also a browser for linked drawings, added to the program in 1994. Few tools from that period are still installable with one command.
entry.caveats: Last SourceForge update was 2013-04-11, it needs X11, and a long-time user mentions quirks from its age.
